title: How to Calculate Time for Payroll and Avoid Getting Underpaid
summary: Learn how to calculate time for payroll accurately with Ontop's expert guide. Avoid underpayment and streamline your international payroll process.

Remote teams, international contractors, and global employees require precise tracking of work hours, overtime calculations, and time-off deductions to ensure accurate payments and compliance with local labor laws. Accurate timesheet calculations and wage computations become critical when dealing with different pay periods, hourly rates, and salary conversions across borders. The right tools eliminate manual spreadsheet work and reduce costly errors that can lead to underpayments or compliance issues, which is why many companies turn to comprehensive payroll software to streamline their international operations. Contractors juggling multiple clients across time zones lose an average of 6 billable hours per month due to forgotten work sessions, incorrect decimal conversions, and missing overtime flags. These aren't dramatic failures. They're 15-minute client calls that vanish from memory by Friday, or 45-minute revision sessions that never make it onto invoices because workers reconstruct their week from fragments instead of logging hours as they happen. Remote workers face documentation challenges that traditional employees never encounter because their work exists only as evidence they create themselves. Without office arrival logs or physical presence confirmation, proving hours worked depends entirely on records contractors maintain independently. Companies implementing structured time-tracking systems see up to an 80% improvement in payroll accuracy, but that advantage disappears when workers wait until the end of the week to fill out timesheets. The gap between work completion and time entry guarantees missing billable hours that represent real income loss, not administrative inconvenience. Cross-border contractors lose money even when time calculations are perfect because the payment infrastructure treats international transfers as exceptions that require manual intervention. Wire transfers can take five to seven business days, charge $25 to $50 in fees, and incur a 3% currency conversion fee before funds reach accounts workers can actually use. Global worker pay fell 12% when adjusted for inflation in 2025, with payment friction and currency volatility contributing significantly to that erosion. The calculation accuracy contractors fought to maintain all month collapses during the final step when legacy banking systems introduced delays and fees that weren't part of the original agreement. Decimal conversion errors create invisible underpayment that compounds across pay periods. Entering 7 hours and 45 minutes as 7.45 hours instead of 7.75 hours results in 18 minutes of pay being removed per occurrence. Repeated daily, that mistake costs six hours monthly, worth $300 at a $50 hourly rate. The IRS reports that 40% of small businesses pay an average penalty of $845 annually for late or incorrect filings, often triggered by these small calculation errors that cascade into tax reporting mistakes. Remote workers demonstrate 35% to 40% higher productivity when time is tracked accurately, but most can't identify which client relationships actually generate sustainable income versus which consume disproportionate hours for modest returns. Without project-level tracking that separates efforts across multiple contracts, workers report accurate total hours but generate incorrect invoices because the distribution across clients is wrong. This problem intensifies when clients span different payment schedules, one paying biweekly in USD while another pays monthly in EUR, and calculation accuracy maintained all month collapses during invoice generation. Payroll software built for global contractors compresses payment cycles from days to seconds across 150+ countries by automating time conversions, currency calculations, and compliance checks that workers used to handle manually. Small Time Tracking Mistakes Can Cost You Real Money Short-term tracking errors add up to real financial loss . A missing 15 minutes , an incorrect break deduction , or a time zone misunderstanding on an international project compounds over weeks and months into paychecks that never arrive and income that disappears . Payroll errors often start during time tracking , not when payment is processed. According to Remote's 2024 Global Payroll Report , 53% of employees have experienced a payroll issue in their careers, and 40% reported experiencing a payroll error within the previous year . Inaccurate time records are a common contributing factor. " 53% of employees have experienced a payroll issue in their careers, and 40% reported experiencing a payroll error within the previous year." — Remote's 2024 Global Payroll Report 🔑 Takeaway: More than half of all workers face payroll problems, with time tracking inaccuracies being a root cause of these costly errors. The Freelancer's Dilemma Many independent professionals juggle multiple clients simultaneously. A designer might work on three projects in one day, a software developer might split time between contract work and meetings, and a marketing consultant might switch between several client accounts throughout the week. Without organized tracking, it becomes easy to forget billable time or miscalculate total hours worked. Freelancers and contractors are responsible for tracking and reporting their own hours: there's no physical clock-in system, payroll department, or manager verifying attendance. Accurate payment depends entirely on personal recordkeeping , and every unrecorded or miscalculated hour is money that may never reach a paycheck. How do time zones create payroll complexity for global workers? Global workers face added complexity. A freelancer in Colombia working with clients in New York, London, and Singapore must navigate misunderstandings around shift times, deadlines, overtime calculations, and pay period cutoffs . An hour worked late on Friday in one country may fall into a different payroll period in another. Manual tracking across spreadsheets breaks down as client bases grow. Timezone conversions introduce errors, and payment delays stretch from days to weeks. What solutions help prevent payroll time errors? Payroll software automatically tracks time and calculates payments across 150+ countries , eliminating timezone confusion and ensuring accurate payments without manual reconciliation. Most payroll-related time errors can be prevented. Workers who receive accurate payments follow a process: track hours in real time , document project work carefully, verify timesheets before submission, and maintain records for discrepancies. Knowing you need accurate records and keeping them under pressure are two different things. How to Calculate Time for Payroll Correctly The math itself isn't complicated: record start and stop times , subtract unpaid breaks , convert minutes to decimals , and sum totals . The challenge is maintaining discipline across fragmented workdays, multiple clients , and shifting project scopes without letting hours slip through the cracks . Accurate time tracking requires consistent habits and the right tools to capture every billable minute . Whether you're using manual timesheets or automated software, the key steps remain the same across all payroll systems. Time Tracking Calculation Process Step 1: Record start/stop times Key details: Use 24-hour format for clarity and consistency Step 2: Subtract unpaid breaks Key details: Deduct lunch breaks and personal time from total hours Step 3: Convert to decimals Key details: Standardize time format (e.g., 15 minutes = 0.25 hours) Step 4: Calculate totals Key details: Sum all daily hours for the full pay period 🎯 Key Point: The most common payroll errors happen during time conversion - always double-check that 30 minutes equals 0.5 hours , not 0.3. "Payroll errors cost businesses an average of $1,100 per employee annually, with time calculation mistakes accounting for 40% of these errors." — American Payroll Association, 2023 ⚠️ Warning: Never round time in favor of the employer without written policies - this violates Fair Labor Standards Act requirements and can result in costly penalties . Record Hours as They Happen, Not Later Freelancers working across three client projects in a single afternoon face a specific trap. They finish a two-hour design session for Client A, jump into a 90-minute strategy call for Client B, then spend an hour revising deliverables for Client C. By Friday, they're trying to remember Tuesday's schedule from calendar fragments and fading memory. One forgotten 45-minute session doesn't feel significant until it happens twice weekly across four clients: six billable hours lost monthly, or roughly $600 to $900 in unreported income for mid-tier contractors. How does delayed time tracking affect accuracy? This pattern appears whether you're a developer splitting time between maintenance contracts and new builds, or a marketing consultant managing simultaneous campaigns. When work sessions blur together, your brain fills in the gaps with approximations that consistently undercount the actual hours worked. Convert Minutes to Decimals Without Rounding Errors Payroll systems process time in decimal format: 15 minutes = 0.25 hours, 30 minutes = 0.5 hours, 45 minutes = 0.75 hours. A common mistake is rounding incorrectly—seven hours and 45 minutes becomes 7.45 hours instead of 7.75 hours. That error, repeated across a month of timesheets, removes 15 hours from your payroll calculation . For someone billing at $50 per hour, that's $750 in lost earnings, invisible because the timesheet you submitted matches the payment you received. Separate Regular Hours from Overtime When It Applies Contractors working under agreements with overtime thresholds must split weekly totals into regular and overtime hours before submission. If your contract pays standard rates for the first 40 hours and time-and-a-half beyond that, a 47-hour work week comprises 40 regular hours plus 7 overtime hours, each calculated at different rates. Modern contractor platforms recognize that accurate payroll processing is a competitive advantage. Solutions like payroll software compress payment cycles from days to seconds across 150+ countries by automating time conversions, currency calculations, and compliance checks that contractors previously handled manually. Track Project-Specific Hours When Working Multiple Contracts A developer maintaining old code for one client while building new features for another must document each contract separately. Monday's six hours might be split into four hours on the maintenance contract and two hours on the new build. Without project-level tracking, you can report accurate total hours but still create incorrect invoices because the distribution across clients is wrong. How do different time zones and payment schedules complicate tracking? This becomes harder when clients are in different time zones with different payment schedules: one pays fortnightly in USD, another monthly in EUR, and a third pays per project milestone in GBP. The accuracy you maintained all month falls apart when creating invoices if you cannot connect specific hours to specific agreements. Most of the time, the problem starts earlier —when the worker miscalculates their own hours before submitting a timesheet or invoice . A simple calculation error on your end can result in weeks of underpayment before the mistake is caught and corrected. 💡 Key Point: The real issue isn't payroll software making mistakes—it's human error in the initial time calculation that sets off a domino effect throughout the payment process . What happens when you forget unpaid work hours? Accurate payroll depends on capturing work when it happens, not reconstructing it from memory. A contractor billing three clients forgets the 15-minute Slack conversation clarifying the project scope, the 20 minutes spent reviewing feedback, and the 10-minute call confirming a deadline. Over a month, these forgotten fragments total eight billable hours: an entire workday never invoiced. How common are payroll errors from incomplete records? According to research from the American Payroll Association , 49% of employees have been affected by a payroll error, often from incomplete worker-submitted records. Client calls, revision requests, administrative tasks, and project coordination are billable work, but they get lost when workers rely on end-of-week memory rather than real-time documentation. What happens when overtime calculations go wrong? Overtime miscalculation occurs when workers fail to distinguish between regular and premium-rate hours. A designer works 42 hours in a week but records all hours at the standard rate because they didn't track which two hours qualified for overtime pay. A developer in Portugal works late to accommodate a New York client's timezone but forgets to flag those evening hours as outside their normal schedule. How do broken deduction errors impact payroll accuracy? Break deductions create similar problems. Workers subtract 30 minutes for lunch when they took 20, or deduct an hour when they worked through lunch entirely. Estimating break time instead of tracking it introduces cumulative errors across pay periods. A contractor who over-deducts breaks by 15 minutes per day loses more than five hours of pay each month. What happens when you convert time incorrectly? Payroll systems process time in decimal format, not hours and minutes. This is where conversion errors cost money. Thirty minutes equals 0.5 hours. Forty-five minutes equals 0.75 hours. Fifteen minutes equals 0.25 hours. A freelancer who worked 7 hours and 45 minutes but enters 7.45 hours instead of 7.75 hours forfeits 18 minutes of pay. How do small conversion errors impact your bottom line? Done daily, that's six hours each month, worth $300 at a $50 hourly rate. The IRS reports that 40% of small businesses pay an average penalty of $845 per year for late or incorrect filings and payments, often triggered by calculation errors that lead to tax reporting mistakes. Most teams handle contractor payments using spreadsheets and manual invoice review. As contractor numbers grow and workers span multiple countries with different tax requirements and payment schedules, errors multiply. title: Turn off your slop cannon
summary: Here's how to write in a way that respects your reader's time and keeps us all from drowning in walls of text.
body_text: Good writing is a gift to everyone around you. Clear, concise communication means your readers spend less time decoding your words and more time acting on them. Here's how to write in a way that respects your reader's time and keeps us all from drowning in walls of text. Why this matters AI slop is real, and we can do better. The internet is full of bloated, padded writing generated (or at least inspired) by AI that optimizes for length over clarity. Don't add to it. When you write vague or wordy content, you're forcing your reader to run your writing through their own AI just to distill what you meant. That's inefficient for everyone and costs tokens once when you write it, and each time someone else has to run your writing through AI just to decode it. Clear writing is a kindness. It's also faster, easier to find, easier to act on, and more accessible to people whose first language isn't English or who use assistive technology. How to structure long-form content Not everything needs to be read front to back. Use progressive disclosure: lead with the essential, then offer more for those who want it. Layer Format Length cap TLDR The elevator pitch. What is this and why does it matter? 2-3 sentences High-level summary The key points, decisions, or recommendations. 2-3 paragraphs Detailed outline or doc Full context, nuance, supporting info. 1-2 pages Tips for tighter writing Cut the filler . "In order to" → "to." "At this point in time" → "now." "Due to the fact that" → "because." Read your draft and delete anything that doesn't add meaning. One idea per sentence . If you need a comma or a semicolon to connect two thoughts, consider whether they should be two sentences instead. Front-load the point . Put the most important information first—in the document, in the section, and in the sentence. Don't make readers wade through context before getting to the answer. Use plain words . "Help" not "assist." "Use" not "utilize." "Start" not "commence." Simpler words are faster to read and more accessible to non-native speakers. Use active voice . "The team reviewed the proposal" not "The proposal was reviewed by the team." Avoid sensory language . "Check the doc" not "see the doc." "Review the table" not "look at the table." Not everyone can see, and inclusive language is clearer language. Prompting guidelines for AI-assisted writing When you use AI to help you write, be specific about the standard you want to hold. Add instructions like: " Make this clear, concise, and succinct. Remove filler words. Use plain language and active voice. Follow accessibility best practices. " If you wouldn't write it yourself, don't publish it just because an AI did. Read what you generate and edit it. Remember, even if AI wrote it, you still own it. The goal isn't fewer words for their own sake—it's more signal per word. Your readers will thank you. I wrote this with AI to prove my point. It only took me a few minutes because I wrote a longer prompt to tighten things up from the start. Then, I only had to do a bit of light editing, mostly to remove the pesky em dashes that AI loves so much. Here's my prompt: " Help me write a company-wide post about being kind to your reader. 1. There's a lot of AI slop out there; don't add to it. 2. It's more efficient (and saves more tokens) if you clean up your writing than if everyone has to use their AI to distill your writing. 3. Tips for writing more succinctly, clearly, concisely, and accessibly. You can look at @helpdocs/.cursor/skills for ideas from our team. a. Include tips about progressive disclosure, offering quick essential info first, then adding more context if a user decides to continue reading, like: first write a TLDR - that's the elevator pitch, then include an executive summary - a more detailed overview, then a detailed outline for those who want the nitty gritty. Make sure to add caps on everything to control the sprawl - TLDR should be 2-3 sentences, exec summary 2-3 paragraphs, detailed outline 1-2 pages. b. Add prompting guidelines that can help tighten up your language, like "It should be clear, concise, succinct, and follow accessibility best practices." The tone should be professional, but also friendly and helpful, not curt, nagging, or snarky. Pretend you're a technical writer arguing for best practices for clear, concise, succinct, accessible writing. This should be 1 page max." You can see that my prompt isn't perfect. But it was enough to guide AI away from producing a pile of slop. Step 3 of the prompt references the technical writing style guide that my team uses. We've built those into skills that we use every time we write with AI. It saves us from having to build that info into our prompt each time. You can build similar skills to achieve the same effect. Digital.gov has a great resource on writing better that you can build into your own skills. title: Maharam Celebrates Mr. Goodman: The Kiteman
summary: This July, Maharam celebrates Mr. Goodman: The Kiteman. A book designed and edited in collaboration with Kite Club—a collective of kite enthusiasts comprising creative director Peter Hebbing,...
body_text: This July, Maharam celebrates Mr. Goodman: The Kiteman . A book designed and edited in collaboration with Kite Club—a collective of kite enthusiasts comprising creative director Peter Hebbing, industrial designer Bertjan Pot, and the photographers Maurice Scheltens and Liesbeth Abbenes—the volume honors the life and work of English engineer turned kite connoisseur Malcolm Goodman. Kite Club first encountered Goodman in a YouTube video. Surrounded by kites he had assembled over the course of more than forty years, Goodman offered his collection to whoever would find it a permanent home. After connecting with Goodman, Kite Club sought to honor his wishes, helping to pack and preserve the kites for posterity while pursuing new ways to share Goodman’s story. The collection of over one thousand kites represents a vast array of typologies from around the globe, from the American “Gibson Girl” kite to the Malaysian wau bulan , and reflects the strong bonds Goodman built with many of the world’s great kite makers. The resulting volume, Mr. Goodman: The Kiteman showcases Goodman’s immense and idiosyncratic collection. Photography by Scheltens & Abbenes highlights a selection of over 280 kites—from intricate miniatures to graphic canvases and the most utilitarian of designs—while also capturing the profusion that occupied the ground floor of Goodman’s home, which once served as a private kite museum. An introductory essay by design historian Emily King draws together anecdotes from Goodman’s life in kiting, while brief essays throughout the book by King and Pot offer context from historical and contemporary kite culture. Mr. Goodman: The Kiteman coincides with an exhibition of the same name at Kunsthal Rotterdam on view through August 30, 2026 About Kite Club Kite Club, formed by creative director Peter Hebbing, industrial designer Bertjan Pot, and the photographers Maurice Scheltens and Liesbeth Abbenes, began with a shared passion for single-line kites and evolved into a collaborative creative outlet. While the collective started with sharing their handmade kites on Instagram, Kite Club now facilitates a range of exhibitions, workshops, and publications, including the 2025 book One Single Kite , which details each stage of a kite-making process. About Maharam Founded in 1902 in New York, Maharam is a leading creator of textiles for commercial and residential interiors. Recognized for its rigorous and holistic commitment to design, Maharam embraces a range of disciplines from product, graphic, and digital design to art and architecture. Maharam textiles are included in the permanent collections of the Art Institute of Chicago, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Stedelijk Museum, among others. Maharam is the recipient of the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum Design Patron Award for its longstanding support of art and design. title: Honeywell Technologies Completes Sale of Warehouse and Workflow Solutions Business to American Industrial Partners | Honeywell Technologies
summary: CHARLOTTE, N.C. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 27, 2026-- Honeywell Technologies ( NASDAQ: HON) today announced it has completed the sale of its Warehouse and Workflow Solutions (WWS) business to American Industrial Partners (AIP) in an all-cash transaction.
body_text: Honeywell Technologies Completes Sale of Warehouse and Workflow Solutions Business to American Industrial Partners Jul 27, 2026 PDF Download 88.6 KB CHARLOTTE, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 27, 2026-- Honeywell Technologies ( NASDAQ: HON ) today announced it has completed the sale of its Warehouse and Workflow Solutions (WWS) business to American Industrial Partners (AIP) in an all-cash transaction. The business operates commercially under the Intelligrated and Transnorm brands. The divestiture of WWS allows Honeywell Technologies to further focus on its pure-play automation portfolio in the Building, Industrial and Process end markets, and the long-term growth opportunities aligned with the industrial sector’s transition from automation to autonomy. "The completion of the WWS divestiture further sharpens Honeywell Technologies as a pure-play automation company," said Vimal Kapur, chairman and CEO of Honeywell Technologies. "We are poised to lead the industrial sector's transition from automation to autonomy, and this sale enables us to focus more fully on that task, accelerating long-term value creation for our customers and shareowners." The completion of this divestiture follows Honeywell Technologies’ spin-off of its Aerospace Technologies business, which is now an independent public company that operates as Honeywell Aerospace (Nasdaq: HONA) as of June 29, 2026. That separation was preceded by Honeywell Technologies’ spin-off of its Advanced Materials business, Solstice Advanced Materials (Nasdaq: SOLS), on October 30, 2025. Since 2023, the company has completed approximately $11.5 billion of accretive, synergistic acquisitions, including Compressor Controls Corporation, SCADAfence, the Access Solutions business from Carrier Global, the LNG business from Air Products, Sundyne, Li-ion Tamer and the Catalyst Technologies business from Johnson Matthey. In addition, the company completed the divestiture of its Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) business in 2025 and has announced the sale of its Productivity Solutions and Services business, with expected closing in early August of 2026. About Honeywell Technologies Honeywell Technologies is a global, pure-play automation company with a legacy of innovating to help solve the world’s most mission-critical challenges, enhancing the quality of life for people and communities around the world. We serve the building, industrial and process sectors with a broad portfolio of services, solutions and products, underpinned by our Honeywell Technologies Accelerator operating system and Honeywell Technologies Forge intelligence layer. By combining the deep domain expertise of our more than 50,000 employees with decades of data from our global installed base, we are uniquely positioned to lead the industrial sector’s transition from automation to autonomy. title: IDEX Health & Science Launches New MarvelXACT™ PEEKsil™ Connection System

body_text: Rohnert Park, California, November 30, 2020 – IDEX Health & Science, industry leader in fluidic connections for life science applications, has launched the new MarvelXACT™ PEEKsil™ Connection Systems. Other bioinert products supplied by IDEX Health & Science include: MarvelX and MarvelXACT connection technology, 1mm columns, bioinert PEEK-Lined Stainless-Steel Column Hardware and a novel flat film degasser. For more information about the new MarvelXACT™ PEEKsil™ Connection System, visit our store. title: How to lock a document as read-only to prevent accidental edits inside a card?
summary: See how to lock a document as read-only to prevent accidental edits inside a card in Jestor.
body_text: Inside Jestor 's document tool, you can lock editing on a text linked to a card, making it available for reading only — preventing someone from accidentally typing into a document that shouldn't be changed anymore. Why do documents linked to a card risk accidental edits? A document connected to a record, like meeting minutes or a summary of a client conversation, often needs to be frozen once it's finalized. If anyone with access can edit it freely, there's a risk that an accidental change could erase or modify already-recorded information. How to lock a document in Jestor? Open the document linked to the card or record. Use the lock-editing option, available in the document's tools. With the document locked, anyone with access can read it but can't type or change the content. If editing is needed again later, simply unlock the document before making the change. Document state What you can do Locked Read-only, no risk of accidental edits Unlocked Normal editing, with every text tool available Why choose Jestor? Since each card can have more than one connected document — minutes on top, a summary below, for example — locking each one individually lets you control exactly which content can still be edited and which is already finalized in Jestor . Frequently Asked Questions Who can unlock a locked document? Whoever has editing access to that document can unlock it when needed. Can a locked document still be shared with other people? Yes, you can add people with access even while the document is locked for editing. Does locking the document prevent viewing the content? No, locking only prevents editing; reading continues to work normally. title: Cross-border Payments: A Technical Implementation Guide
summary: Design cross-border payments with a core ledger, rail orchestration, FX controls, reconciliation, and compliance checkpoints at every hop
body_text: Where is the money right now? That is the only question that matters in a cross-border payment system. On 27 February 2025, the ECB's TARGET Services outage showed how many teams couldn't respond when their T2 and T2S were unavailable for approximately 10 and 8 hours. When T2 went down, interbank settlements stalled, and engineers were piecing the picture together from SWIFT messages, nostro statements, and PSP files arriving on different timelines and in different formats. The cross-border payment corridor was frozen for hours before anyone had the full picture. The outage was difficult to contain because cross-border payments lack a single system of record. A payment passes through multiple intermediaries, foreign exchange (FX) legs, and message formats, each with its own clock and its own record. Engineering, finance, and compliance teams all depend on a single solution to track, move, and reconcile funds across jurisdictions. A core ledger serves as the single solution for cross-border payments, acting as a system of record separate from the rails that move funds while supporting engineering, finance, and compliance teams. What are cross-border payments? Cross-border payments are fund transfers in which the payer and payee are in different jurisdictions or countries and may involve different currencies. The FX legs drive most of the engineering complexity because you are dealing with a patchwork of legal regimes, compliance obligations, capital controls, and supervisory authorities. Three categories shape how you construct and execute cross-border payments: Wholesale payments move between financial institutions and are generally high-value; in some operational monitoring frameworks, wholesale payments are defined as USD $100,000 or more. The IMF puts the wholesale cross-border payments market at about $145 trillion . Retail payments are low-value end-user transfers (P2P, P2B, or B2B) across jurisdictions. They are lower-value and higher-volume, making retail payments relatively expensive and slow. Remittances are a retail sub-segment, usually regular low-value transfers to emerging markets. Settlement occurs through several CPMI payment models, including correspondent banking (respondent and correspondent banks adjusting nostro/vostro balances via SWIFT), interlinking separate payment systems across jurisdictions, and newer peer-to-peer rails, including digital assets. The four steps to build a cross-border payment system Building a cross-border payment system requires you to map your use cases and corridors, design a cross-border ledger, implement APIs, routing, FX, and reconciliation flows, and embed compliance, fraud controls, and observability into the system. The order matters. Map corridors first so provider-specific assumptions don't leak into your core. Build the ledger next to anchor the system of record before any rail-specific code is written. Then add normalization, routing, FX, and reconciliation around it to move the money and keep the books clean. Update the flow with compliance and observability to ensure every payment is processed correctly. Step 1: Map your cross-border payment use cases and corridors A corridor is an origin-destination pair, so map only the cross-border payment corridors you actually serve. Each one carries its own rails, partners, settlement windows, and failure modes. For example, USD-to-MXN is a different engineering problem than EUR-to-INR. If you treat cross-border payment corridors generically, provider-specific logic ends up in the product code. For each corridor, document the rails available to you and their issues: SWIFT correspondent banking reaches 200+ countries and 11,000+ banks, and about 80% of the total journey time happens after the message leaves the SWIFT network. The post-SWIFT leg is your dominant production failure mode. Local instant schemes settle in seconds or near real-time within their domestic boundary. Reaching local schemes across borders requires a local partner or an interlinking arrangement. Card push rails can be an option for selected payout corridors, with performance depending on corridor, issuer, and receiving institution. Stablecoin rails can be an option for selected corridors, with performance depending on network, corridor, and settlement model, and with the caveat that stablecoin payments do not achieve the same finality as central bank reserve settlement. Build a corridor-to-rail matrix, so you know which rails you can depend on for each corridor and where you need fallback routes. It also tells you, before you write any code, how many distinct message formats and settlement timelines your ledger will have to absorb. Step 2: Design a cross-border ledger and money movement core The ledger collects user balances , settlement accounts, FX legs, and fees, while the rails move the funds. Separating ledger and rails lets you swap a payout partner in one corridor without rewriting product logic in another, and it keeps rail-specific behavior at the edge instead of spreading through product code. Define payment orders and ledger entries as shared primitives, with accounts governed by the same model, and use immutable posted orders with double-entry auditability and zero-sum error detection so the platform can scale to new payment types and geographies without re-architecture. Two invariants make the ledger trustworthy, and both have to be enforced at the database or API boundary: Double-entry at write time Every financial event creates at least two postings that sum to zero, and no code path can bypass this rule. Enforcing double-entry only in application code leaves too much room for silent failures. Immutability through reversal postings Posted entries stay fixed, so a mistake is fixed with a reversal posting. The append-only log makes retroactive changes detectable; altering a past entry requires rewriting everything downstream of that entry. Build balances as materialized views over the immutable postings, and treat postings as the primary source of truth. Intermediate clearing accounts should normally return to zero; a non-zero balance is an unresolved state you need to investigate. A programmable ledger, paired with rail connectivity and orchestration, is the system of record for cross-border money movement. Formance is an open-source, programmable core ledger that unifies fiat and digital assets with regulatory-grade traceability, so the same posting model holds whether a payment settles over SWIFT, a local scheme, or an on-chain transfer. Step 3: Implement APIs, routing, FX, and reconciliation for cross-border payments Implement normalization, routing, FX, and reconciliation around the ledger. Normalize external formats before routing ISO 20022 MX became the exclusive standard for cross-border payment instructions on SWIFT on 22 November 2025. Legacy MT instructions and statements, therefore, need to be translated into the relevant MX or CAMT family, and each translation should be explicit in your internal model. Aligning your field names, identifiers, and reconciliation logic with ISO 20022 primitives reduces downstream translation costs. On-chain transfers require chain-specific normalization. This includes transaction records, event logs, fees, and confirmation states. These elements do not map cleanly to a payment record, so you need to parse them into internal postings and account for failed, replaced, or reorganized transaction states at the edge. Make every posting idempotent by keying it to the source event ID, so that a retried or replayed message commits exactly once rather than double-posting the same payment. Route each payment A routing layer should select a partner based on payment attributes and corridor objectives, such as straight-through processing rate and cost. Add validation before committing so obvious downstream rejection conditions are caught earlier. Operational inputs worth evaluating include corridor-level rejection rates, bank cut-off times, liquidity, FX spread changes, and beneficiary bank settlement reliability. Within a corridor, the engine can choose among available local schemes instead of treating all payouts as the same route. Book FX as linked legs An FX conversion routes through a conversion account and an FX counterparty, with the spread posted to revenue as its own leg. Modeling FX as explicit postings keeps the accounting trail defensible at audit. Reconcile against every source A payment can settle on an external rail before your books are clean, while reconciliation is the control process that ties bank, PSP, FX, and ledger records back to the same event. For FX, reconcile across bank/trade data, ledger entries, and booked rates, then verify that the booked rate reflects the agreed trade rate. Expect timing gaps because nostro banks may not notify you until later on the settlement day or the next working day, and correspondent statements often arrive as delayed messages. Set tolerance windows based on your own observed payout-clearance distribution rather than on a guess. You need compliance, fraud controls, and observability to prove it moved correctly. Step 4: Embed compliance, fraud controls, and observability into cross-border flows Compliance, fraud controls, and observability sit at specific checkpoints inside the flow of funds, and every money movement in a correspondent chain carries its own obligation. Compliance at three points Place compliance screening at three points: Onboarding: This starting point involves identifying and verifying the customer's and beneficial owner's identities, understanding the purpose and nature of the business relationship, and conducting ongoing due diligence. Sanctions screening is addressed under separate FATF recommendations. Payment initiation and pre-settlement: The Travel Rule (FATF Recommendation 16, revised June 2025) requires that originator and beneficiary information accompany the transfer and be submitted concurrently. Per-transaction: In correspondent chains, bank AML/CFT checks happen at each institution before a payment can be completed. Speed does not remove the need for sanctions and financial crime controls before funds are credited. Reflect licensing and data obligations in where systems run and how data is stored. Retention requirements vary across corridors. Records should be kept for 10 years from the date of the transaction, and a single corridor can require data held across multiple jurisdictions with different retention clocks. Fraud controls to check legitimate transactions Fraud controls run alongside AML and sanctions screening, not as a replacement for them. While compliance asks whether a party is permitted to transact, fraud controls ask whether the transaction itself appears legitimate. Score payments at initiation using velocity, device, and behavioral signals, and pull in beneficiary risk signals from corridor history, prior chargebacks, and recalls. Decisions should be explicit postings or metadata on the payment order so the reason a transaction was held, stepped up, or released is auditable later. Feed confirmed fraud back into the routing layer so that repeat patterns, mule accounts, and high-risk beneficiaries get blocked earlier on the next attempt, rather than being caught again downstream. Observability for complete monitoring For observability, track cross-border payment states, corridor-level latency, failure patterns, and reconciliation breaks in production. The Financial Stability Board (FSB) cross-border payments program will require every PSP to surface expected delivery time, tracking status, and terms of service by the end of 2027. Because most of the journey time occurs at the final stage, you must instrument the full payment path, including network transit and domestic delivery. Monitoring should alert on known thresholds, and observability should preserve identifiers, timestamps and partner responses. Preserve the ledger context needed to debug new failure modes, such as latency spikes during cross-border settlement or race conditions in orchestration. Treat long-lived clearing balances as an operational signal that a persistent balance points to a clearing issue you have not resolved. A proactive cross-border payment The example below shows Steps 2 and 3 working together on a single remittance: Carlos in Houston sends money to Rosa in Guadalajara, funded by ACH, bridged from USD to USDC, converted to MXN, and paid out locally. The accounts model that holds what is at each stage. Real-world party Ledger account Holds Carlos's funded balance @users:carlos:wallet Carlos's available USD funds USDC on-ramp counterparty @counterparties:onramp:provider_a running balance against the USD/USDC on-ramp Carlos's USDC custody @users:carlos:provider_a:custody USDC held before FX conversion FX counterparty @counterparties:fxProviders:provider_a running balance against the FX provider The conversion @exchanges:conv:RMT001 transient funds mid-conversion Carlos's payout balance @users:carlos:local_bank:payout MXN earmarked for Rosa's payout Platform FX revenue @platform:revenue:fx the spread you keep First, cash enters via the ACH bank rail into Carlos's USD wallet. Next, the platform converts his USD balance one-for-one into USDC via an on-ramp counterparty, resulting in 500 USDC held in the external provider's custody. Then Carlos converts that 500 USDC to MXN: the 500 USDC move to the FX provider, the provider delivers 8,600 MXN into the conversion account at the wholesale execution rate of 17.20, the platform pays Rosa 8,400 MXN at the customer rate of 16.80, it quoted her, and books the 200 MXN difference as spread revenue. The three transactions below are written in Numscript , Formance's domain-specific language for expressing money movements as atomic, double-entry postings on the ledger. // WALLET_TOPUP // Event: Carlos funds his wallet; cash enters via the ACH bank rail send [USD/2 50000] ( source = @platform:banks:us_bank:main allowing unbounded overdraft destination = @users:carlos:wallet ) set_tx_meta ( "event_type" , "wallet_topup" ) set_tx_meta ( "remittance_id" , "RMT001" ) // USD_TO_USDC // Event: Carlos's USD wallet balance is bridged 1:1 into USDC in external provider custody send [USD/2 50000] ( source = @users:carlos:wallet destination = @counterparties:onramp:provider_a ) send [USDC/6 500000000] ( source = @counterparties:onramp:provider_a allowing unbounded overdraft destination = @users:carlos:provider_a:custody ) set_tx_meta ( "event_type" , "usd_to_usdc" ) set_tx_meta ( "remittance_id" , "RMT001" ) set_tx_meta ( "bridge_rate" , "1.00" ) // FX_CONVERT // Event: Carlos converts 500 USDC to MXN. The FX provider executes at 17.20 (wholesale); // the platform quotes Rosa 16.80 (customer rate) and keeps the 0.40 MXN/USDC markup as revenue (200 MXN total). send [USDC/6 500000000] ( source = @users:carlos:provider_a:custody destination = @counterparties:fxProviders:provider_a ) send [MXN/2 860000] ( source = @counterparties:fxProviders:provider_a allowing unbounded overdraft destination = @exchanges:conv:RMT001 ) send [MXN/2 840000] ( source = @exchanges:conv:RMT001 destination = @users:carlos:local_bank:payout ) send [MXN/2 20000] ( source = @exchanges:conv:RMT001 destination = @platform:revenue:fx ) set_tx_meta ( "event_type" , "fx_convert" ) set_tx_meta ( "remittance_id" , "RMT001" ) set_tx_meta ( "customer_rate" , "16.80" ) set_tx_meta ( "execution_rate" , "17.20" ) Each conversion records as one atomic entry: the ledger commits all legs or none. The USD-to-USDC bridge posts as its own transaction so the asset change is explicit and auditable, and the FX spread posts to revenue as its own leg (difference between the 17.20 wholesale rate the platform executes at and the 16.80 customer rate quoted to Rosa) with both rates riding along as metadata. When the three-way reconciliation runs the next morning, the on-ramp bridge, the execution rate booked, the customer rate quoted, the spread kept, and the payout earmarked are already on the ledger, traceable to one remittance ID, enough to prove the FX gain from the remittance ID and ledger metadata alone. Where is the money in your cross-border payments system? Can you confirm right now, without opening a PSP report, where each multi-currency, multi-rail balance is located? If the answer is no, you are one rail outage away from ECB's TARGET Services outage; reconstructing the picture from SWIFT messages and nostro statements while the corridor stayed frozen for hours. The hard part is not building a ledger, an integration layer, an orchestration engine, and a reconciliation process in isolation. It is wiring these modules together so a cross-border payment commits atomically across all four and still ties back to one event at audit. That integration is a multi-year program in-house. Formance ships it as a single stack, so your engineers write the flow once in Numscript, and the same auditable record applies whether funds settle via SWIFT, SEPA Instant, or on-chain.
